member.name: T:Orchard.Mirror.Media.AacEldAudioCapture
member.summary: Receives the paired CoreDevice audio leg and records its AAC-ELD access units to a file.

remarks.para: This does not play anything, and deliberately so. The device sends AAC-ELD (AudioStreamMode=8, 48 kHz stereo, 480-sample frames) and Windows has no decoder for it — Media Foundation's AAC decoder covers LC and HE only. ADR 0014 §6 requires Orchard's own decoder rather than a vendored codec, and that decoder does not exist yet.

What blocks writing it is a reference recording: an AAC-ELD stream cannot be synthesised locally, because no encoder for it is installed and its access units carry no sync word to re-frame from. So this class exists to produce the input the decoder work needs, and to prove the leg is wired end to end, without pretending to be playback.
The output is length-prefixed access units — a 4-byte big-endian length before each — the same shape eng/orchard-mirror/analyze-rtp-capture.py already reads for video.

member.name: T:Orchard.Mirror.Media.AacEldAudioLeg
member.summary: Turns the paired CoreDevice audio leg's RTP datagrams into AAC-ELD access units.

remarks.para: The device answers start-audio-stream with RxPayloadType=101 and AudioStreamMode=8, which is Apple AAC-ELD at 48 kHz stereo — see for the frame length, which is not what it is usually reported to be. Unlike the video leg there is no fragmentation and no aggregation scheme: one RTP payload is exactly one access unit, carried raw with no AU-header section, so this class is framing and loss accounting rather than a depacketizer.

Loss is counted rather than concealed. A dropped 10 ms frame is inaudible on its own, but the count is what tells an operator whether silence means "no audio playing" or "the stream is falling apart", and the highest sequence number is what the agent's RTCP receiver reports back — without which the device reaps the audio session after about twenty seconds.

member.remarks: Measured off the device, not read from a cookie. The RTP timestamp advances by exactly 480 per packet on a 48 kHz clock, and feeding 200 real access units to a reference decoder configured for 480 decodes all 200 cleanly at full scale, while configuring it for 512 manages 50 before failing to parse. member.name: P:Orchard.Mirror.Media.AacEldAudioLeg.AudioSpecificConfig
member.summary: The AudioSpecificConfig an AAC-ELD decoder must be initialised with for this stream: AOT 39, 48 kHz, stereo, and the frame length in .

remarks.para: Apple calls this the magic cookie. It is fixed for the mode the device negotiates, so it is stated here rather than parsed out of a stream that never carries it.

This is not the value the ecosystem uses. pymobiledevice3 hardcodes F8 E6 40 00 — as does ADR 0014 §6, which took it from there — and that value sets frameLengthFlag to 0, declaring 512-sample frames. The device sends 480. A reference decoder given F8 E6 40 00 fails on real access units; given F8 E6 50 00 it decodes them all. pymobiledevice3 gets away with it because it also passes AudioToolbox mFramesPerPacket = 480 alongside the cookie.

member.name: T:Orchard.Mirror.Media.HevcDepacketizer
member.summary:
Reassembles RFC 7798 RTP/HEVC payloads into whole NAL units.
Three packet shapes carry video. A payload whose type is below 48 is a single NAL unit and is emitted as-is. Type 48 is an aggregation packet holding several length-prefixed NAL units. Type 49 is a fragmentation unit, one NAL unit spread over consecutive packets, which this class buffers until the end fragment arrives.
The instance is stateful because fragment reassembly spans packets. Feed payloads in arrival order and call when the stream restarts.

member.name: F:Orchard.Mirror.Media.HevcDepacketizer.DisplayServiceTrailer
member.summary: Apple's DisplayService appends this fixed 14-byte footer after a coded-slice NAL. It is not part of the HEVC bitstream — Apple's own receiver strips it before decoding, and a plain RFC 7798 reassembly would hand it to the decoder as trailing slice data. It is matched as an exact suffix, so this is a no-op on any stream that does not carry it.

member.name: P:Orchard.Mirror.Media.HevcDepacketizer.DroppedFragments
member.summary: Number of fragmented NAL units abandoned because a fragment went missing.

member.name: M:Orchard.Mirror.Media.HevcDepacketizer.Reset
member.summary: Forget any half-reassembled fragment. Call when the stream restarts.

member.name: M:Orchard.Mirror.Media.HevcDepacketizer.Depacketize(System.ReadOnlySpan{System.Byte},System.Collections.Generic.List{System.Byte[]})
member.summary: Depacketize one RTP payload, appending every NAL unit it completes to . A payload that only continues a fragment appends nothing. Malformed payloads are discarded rather than throwing — these come off a socket, and one bad datagram must not stop the stream.

member.name: M:Orchard.Mirror.Media.HevcDepacketizer.ReadAggregationPacket(System.ReadOnlySpan{System.Byte},System.Collections.Generic.List{System.Byte[]})
member.summary:
RFC 7798 §4.4.2: a 2-byte payload header, then repeated 16-bit-length-prefixed NAL units.
The DONL/DOND fields are only present when sprop-max-don-diff is greater than zero, which requires out-of-band signalling that Apple's DisplayService does not use. A stream that did carry them would misparse here, so the sizes are bounds-checked and a payload that does not divide cleanly is abandoned rather than emitting garbage NAL units.

member.name: M:Orchard.Mirror.Media.HevcDepacketizer.ReadFragmentationUnit(System.ReadOnlySpan{System.Byte},System.Collections.Generic.List{System.Byte[]})
member.summary:
RFC 7798 §4.4.3: a 2-byte payload header, then a 1-byte FU header carrying a start bit, an end bit, and the real NAL unit type of the fragmented unit.
The reassembled NAL unit header is the payload header with its type field replaced by the FU header's type, so layer id and temporal id survive.

member.name: T:Orchard.Mirror.Media.MirrorStreamMonitor
member.summary: Decides whether a quiet stream means the phone is asleep, the decoder is stuck, or the session is gone.

remarks.para: A dark phone and a dead session are indistinguishable from the stream alone: both simply stop sending. The discriminator is the CoreDevice tunnel, so the caller probes it when says the answer matters, and passes the result in.

Getting this wrong is expensive rather than cosmetic. A sleeping iPhone stops advertising RemotePairing entirely, so once the session is dropped there is nothing left to rediscover over Wi-Fi — treating sleep as a lost session strands the user until they pick the phone up.
